lines.en: Raj, **have you ever been to** Japan? I’m planning a trip next spring.
lines.pt: Raj, você já esteve no Japão? Estou planejando uma viagem para a próxima primavera.

lines.en: Yes! **I’ve been to** Tokyo twice. **I’ve never** seen such clean trains anywhere else.
lines.pt: Sim! Já estive em Tóquio duas vezes. Nunca vi trens tão limpos em nenhum outro lugar.

lines.en: Really? What was the best thing you did there?
lines.pt: Sério? Qual foi a melhor coisa que você fez lá?

lines.en: **I’ve tried** ramen at a tiny shop near the station. It was the best meal of my life.
lines.pt: Eu comi ramen numa lojinha perto da estação. Foi a melhor refeição da minha vida.

lines.en: Wow. **Have you ever** felt lost there? I don’t speak any Japanese.
lines.pt: Nossa. Você já se sentiu perdido lá? Eu não falo nada de japonês.

lines.en: Once, but people helped me. **I’ve never** met anyone unfriendly on my trips.
lines.pt: Uma vez, mas as pessoas me ajudaram. Nunca conheci ninguém antipático nas minhas viagens.

lines.en: That’s reassuring. I’ve never traveled alone before, so I’m a little nervous.
lines.pt: Isso é tranquilizador. Eu nunca viajei sozinha antes, então estou um pouco nervosa.

lines.en: You’ll be fine! Have you ever visited another country by yourself?
lines.pt: Você vai ficar bem! Você já visitou outro país sozinha?

lines.en: Only Finland, for a conference. So this will be my first big adventure.
lines.pt: Só a Finlândia, para uma conferência. Então essa vai ser minha primeira grande aventura.

pages.title: Experiences (present perfect)

situation.text: At a café, a friend asks about your travel experiences before a big trip. You share what you have done, what you have never done and one short story.

pages.goal: By the end of the class you can ask about life experiences, answer with “I’ve been to / I’ve never…” and add one detail in the past.
canDo: Say what you have or have never done
Say how many times: once, twice, a few times
Add details about one experience in the past
success: I ask a Have you ever… question.
I answer with I’ve… or I’ve never…
I add one detail in the past.
I react to my partner’s story.
pages.think: Think of one place or thing you have experienced that most people you know have not. How would you tell that story in English?

Mostre os 4 critérios.
group: Cada estudante diz um país que já visitou ou quer visitar.
Anote no quadro.
extra: What is the farthest place you have been to?
What is on your travel wish list?
support: Aceite palavras soltas (a country, a food) e reformule em frases.

pages.title: Cultural snapshot — Travel stories
pages.intro: Sharing travel stories is an easy way to connect with people in English-speaking countries. Look and guess before you read.

cards.note: A very common question to start a friendly conversation about travel.

cards.en: Tell the story in the past
cards.note: After “Have you ever…?”, people give details with the past: “I went in July.”
Listeners often ask for recommendations: “What would you recommend?”

qs.q: Why do people ask “Have you ever been to…?”
qs.pt: Por que as pessoas perguntam “Have you ever been to…?”

levels.A2: To start a conversation about places you know.
levels.B1: It invites the other person to share experiences and gives you topics to talk about.
levels.B2: It is a low-pressure way to build rapport, since everyone has some travel story or wish.

qs.q: What tense do we use for the details of a trip?
qs.pt: Qual tempo usamos para os detalhes de uma viagem?

levels.A2: The past simple: I went there in 2022.
levels.B1: We use present perfect for the experience and past simple for when and what happened.
levels.B2: Present perfect introduces the experience; past simple anchors it in time with details.

qs.q: What can you ask after someone tells a travel story?
qs.pt: O que perguntar depois de uma história de viagem?

levels.A2: What was the best part? Would you go again?
levels.B1: How was it? What would you recommend?
levels.B2: What surprised you most? Is there anything you would do differently?

pages.compare: In Brazil, travel stories are also popular, especially about beaches and family trips. In English, the questions “Have you ever…?” and “What was it like?” are a ready-made way to keep the talk going. What do you usually ask?

teach.goal: Ver as experiências de viagem como assunto social e a combinação present perfect + past simple.
solo: Mostre os 3 cartões e peça hipóteses.
Pergunte que histórias o estudante gosta de ouvir.
group: Cada estudante escolhe um cartão e explica.
Debate: “Do you agree?”
answers: Q3: What was it like? / What would you recommend?
extra: What is your best travel story?
Do you like hearing other people’s stories?
support: Use as respostas A1 como andaime.
stretch: B2: explique por que present perfect não aceita “yesterday”.

pages.title: Pronunciation lab — natural American English
pages.tip: “Have” and “been” lose strength in fast speech: “I’ve” is quick, “been” is /bɪn/, and “ever” links to “you”.

own.prompt: Write a Have you ever… question about something you really want to know.
own.criteria: Say it twice: slowly, then reduced. Did “been” sound short?

teach.goal: UM só fenômeno: redução de have/been e ligação.
solo: Escutar e identificar → repetir → pergunta própria.
Bata palmas nas sílabas fortes.
group: Coro, depois duplas.
Cada estudante cria uma pergunta.
answers: Identify 1: Have you ever been there? · Identify 2: I’ve never been to Tokyo.
support: Reduza a velocidade e conte as batidas.

levels.h: Controlled practice — choose the best answer

items.q: 1. You want to ask about travel experience.
opts: Have you ever been to Brazil?

items.q: 2. You have never eaten sushi. What do you say?
3. You visited Paris in 2021. Which sentence gives a detail?
opts: I have gone to Paris in 2021.
items.why: With a finished time (in 2021) use the past simple.

items.q: 4. A friend says “I’ve been to Rome!” What do you ask next?
items.why: What was it like? asks for details.

levels.h: Guided practice — complete, substitute and transform

items.why: been is the participle of be.

items.text: I’ve ___ eaten Indian food. I love it!
items.why: often goes between have and the participle.

ans: Have you ever been to Japan?
items.model: Have you ever been to Japan?

opts: Yes, I traveled alone yesterday ever.

teach.goal: Do controlado ao guiado antes da fala livre.

Peça a versão negativa e a pergunta.
group: Duplas comparam antes de revelar.
Pontos por resposta justificada.

pages.title: Group mission — find what you have in common
pages.goal: Each group must discover travel experiences and plan one trip suggestion together.

missions.mission: Find three places that everyone in your group has been to, or three that nobody has visited.
missions.constraint: Ask at least two Have you ever…? questions.

missions.mission: Find one food everyone has tried and one nobody has tried. Recommend one.
missions.constraint: Use “I’ve never…” and “What was it like?”

missions.mission: Find one thing nobody has done and invent a group adventure.
missions.constraint: Use “twice or a few times” and “for the first time”.

success: Answer with I’ve… or I’ve never…

teach.goal: Usar experiências de vida para encontrar pontos em comum.
group: Cada grupo recebe papéis e restrição.
Progressão: com chunks, só palavras-chave, sem roteiro.
Anote 2–3 correções prioritárias.
answers: Modelo: “Have you ever been to Mexico?” → “Yes, twice. It was great.” → “What was it like?”
extra: What did you learn about your classmates?
support: Dê o início de frase em cada cartão.

pages.title: Writing — a small real-life task
pages.task: Write a short message to a friend about one travel experience: where you have been, how many times and one detail.
pages.model: Hi Nina! I’ve been to Tokyo twice. The first time I went in spring, and it was beautiful. I’ve never eaten better ramen! Have you ever been to Asia?
checklist: I asked a Have you ever… question.
pages.tip: Fix only 2–3 priority points and show a more natural way to say the same idea.

teach.goal: Produção escrita curta ligada à situação.
solo: Corrija 2–3 pontos prioritários.
group: Troquem os textos entre colegas.
extra: Add one more experience to your message.

criteria.name: Fluency
criteria.desc: Mantém a comunicação sem interrupções excessivas.

criteria.name: Language use
criteria.desc: Utiliza adequadamente padrões, vocabulário e expressões.

criteria.name: Pronunciation
criteria.desc: É compreensível e usa ritmo e entonação adequados.

criteria.name: Interaction
criteria.desc: Responde, pergunta, esclarece e desenvolve a conversa.

interpret.text: Needs more support. Revisit the main patterns with guided practice before the next lesson.
Functional performance. Work on the lowest criteria in the next lesson.
Good control. Add follow-up questions and longer answers.
Strong performance. Move to a more demanding situation.

pages.title: Level up — the same situation from A1 to C2
pages.intro: The situation stays the same; the language grows in length, nuance and autonomy.

ladder.goal: Name a place and an opinion in short phrases.

ladder.say: I’ve been to Japan twice. It was great.
ladder.goal: Talk about experiences with I’ve been / never.

ladder.say: I’ve been to Japan twice, and I’d really like to go back in autumn.
Having been to Japan twice, I can say the trains are even better than people claim.
Having travelled there a couple of times, I can honestly say it changed how I think about public space.
Few trips have left me as quietly astonished as those two weeks in Kyoto.

pages.note: This progression is illustrative: complex sentences do not define a level on their own. CEFR also considers comprehension, autonomy, fluency, accuracy, interaction and appropriateness.

teach.goal: Mostrar a progressão sem criar seis metodologias.
